section.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About Apatinib (Rivoceranib) for Third-Line Gastric Cancer
section.intro: These FAQs explain how apatinib (rivoceranib) is used as a later-line targeted therapy for advanced gastric cancer, including who it may suit, its benefits, risks, cost, and how international patients can explore access.

items.q: What is apatinib (rivoceranib) for gastric cancer?
items.a: Apatinib, also known as rivoceranib, is an oral targeted therapy approved in China for advanced gastric cancer that has progressed after earlier treatments. It is a small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor that blocks VEGFR-2, a receptor involved in tumour blood vessel growth. It is generally considered for third-line use, meaning after at least two prior lines of chemotherapy. Suitability depends on cancer type, stage, previous treatment, and specialist review.

items.q: How does apatinib work against stomach cancer?
items.a: Apatinib works by blocking VEGFR-2, a signal that tumours use to build new blood vessels and grow. By interfering with this pathway, called angiogenesis, apatinib may slow tumour blood supply and progression in advanced gastric cancer. It is taken as a daily oral tablet rather than by infusion. It does not cure the disease, and how well it works varies between patients and should be assessed by the treating oncology team.

items.q: Is apatinib the same as rivoceranib?
items.a: Yes, apatinib and rivoceranib refer to the same VEGFR-2 targeted drug, with the name differing by region and manufacturer. In China it is widely known as apatinib and was approved for advanced gastric cancer after prior therapy. Rivoceranib is the name often used in international studies and other markets. Because naming and approvals differ by country, patients should confirm the exact product and its approved use with their oncology team.

items.q: Why is apatinib called China's approved targeted therapy?
items.a: Apatinib is described this way because China's drug regulator approved it for third-line advanced gastric cancer, making it one of the first oral VEGFR-2 inhibitors cleared for this setting. This approval was based on trials showing modest improvements in progression control for selected patients. Its regulatory status differs elsewhere, so availability outside China varies. Any decision to use it should follow specialist review of the patient's diagnosis and prior treatment history.

items.q: Who is eligible for apatinib in third-line gastric cancer?
items.a: Apatinib may be considered for adults with advanced or metastatic gastric or gastro-oesophageal junction cancer that has progressed after at least two prior lines of chemotherapy. Eligibility depends on cancer type, stage, overall health, organ function, blood pressure control, and specialist review. Patients with uncontrolled bleeding, severe hypertension, or poor performance status may not be suitable. Final decisions about starting apatinib should always be made by the treating oncology team.

items.q: Is apatinib suitable for all gastric cancer patients?
items.a: No, apatinib is not suitable for all gastric cancer patients and is generally reserved for later-line treatment after other options. It may be considered for selected patients whose disease has progressed despite prior chemotherapy and who remain well enough for treatment. Factors such as bleeding risk, blood pressure, kidney and liver function, and overall condition affect suitability. A qualified oncology team should review each case before recommending apatinib.

items.q: What are the benefits of apatinib for advanced gastric cancer?
items.a: Apatinib may help slow disease progression in some patients with advanced gastric cancer who have run out of standard chemotherapy options. As an oral tablet, it can be taken at home, which some patients find more convenient than infusions. Reported benefits in trials were modest and varied between individuals, and it is not a cure. The likely benefit for any patient should be discussed realistically with the treating oncology team.

items.q: What are the side effects and risks of apatinib?
items.a: Common side effects of apatinib include high blood pressure, protein in the urine, hand-foot syndrome, fatigue, and reduced blood counts. Less common but serious risks include bleeding, blood clots, and problems with wound healing, linked to its effect on blood vessels. Side effects can sometimes be managed with dose adjustments or supportive care. Any new or severe symptoms should be reported promptly, and treatment should be supervised by an oncology team.

items.q: How is apatinib taken and monitored?
items.a: Apatinib is taken as a daily oral tablet, usually at a consistent time after a meal, with the dose set by the treating oncologist. Patients are typically monitored for blood pressure, urine protein, blood counts, and liver and kidney function during treatment. Imaging scans are used periodically to assess whether the cancer is responding. Doses may be paused or reduced if side effects develop, based on the medical team's assessment.

items.q: How much does apatinib treatment cost?
items.a: The cost of apatinib varies widely depending on country, dose, treatment duration, and whether it is locally approved or imported. In China, where it is approved, it is often more accessible than in markets where it must be sourced specially. Final costs also depend on hospital, monitoring tests, supportive care, and any complications. Patients should request a written estimate and confirm pricing with the treating hospital, as figures are not fixed.

Apatinib's availability in India can vary and may depend on regulatory status, importation, and individual hospital arrangements. It is not as widely established in routine third-line use as in China, so access is not guaranteed. Patients interested in apatinib should ask their oncologist about local availability, approved alternatives, and whether importation is possible. Because rules change over time, current availability should be confirmed directly with the treating hospital or pharmacy.

items.q: Which countries offer apatinib for gastric cancer?
items.a: Apatinib is most established in China, where it is approved for third-line advanced gastric cancer, and rivoceranib has been studied in several international trials. Availability in other countries depends on local regulatory approval, importation rules, and hospital practice, and it may not be routinely offered everywhere. Patients considering treatment abroad should confirm current approval status and access with the specific hospital, as regulations differ between countries and change over time.

items.q: How can international patients access apatinib?
items.a: International patients may access apatinib by exploring treatment at centres in countries where it is approved, subject to medical review and hospital acceptance. Access depends on the patient's diagnosis, prior treatment, travel fitness, visa approval, and the hospital's assessment, none of which can be guaranteed in advance. Gathering medical reports and obtaining a specialist second opinion helps clarify whether apatinib is appropriate. Final treatment decisions rest with the treating oncology team.

items.q: Is apatinib used with other treatments?
items.a: Apatinib is sometimes studied in combination with chemotherapy or immunotherapy, though its established approval in gastric cancer is as a single oral agent in the third-line setting. Combination approaches are mainly explored within clinical trials or specialist protocols and are not standard for every patient. Whether a combination is appropriate depends on cancer type, biomarkers, prior treatment, and overall health, and should be decided by a qualified oncology team.

items.q: Are there clinical trials involving apatinib or rivoceranib?
items.a: Yes, apatinib and rivoceranib have been evaluated in clinical trials for gastric and other cancers, some testing combinations with immunotherapy or chemotherapy. Trial eligibility is decided only after medical record review and investigator assessment, and enrolment or benefit cannot be guaranteed. Trials often have strict inclusion and exclusion criteria based on stage, prior treatment, and organ function. Patients interested in trials should discuss current options with their oncology team.

If apatinib stops controlling the cancer, the oncology team may reassess options based on the patient's condition, prior treatments, and biomarker profile. Possible next steps can include other targeted therapies, immunotherapy, further chemotherapy, clinical trials, or a focus on supportive and symptom-directed care. There is no single right answer, and choices depend on individual circumstances. These decisions should be made together with a qualified oncology team after reviewing scans and overall health.

items.q: What medical reports are needed to explore apatinib treatment?
items.a: To explore apatinib, doctors typically need recent pathology reports confirming gastric cancer, imaging scans such as CT or PET-CT, and a summary of prior chemotherapy and responses. Blood tests showing liver, kidney, and blood-count status, along with details of blood pressure and other health conditions, are also useful. Complete records help specialists judge suitability and reduce delays. The treating oncology team decides what additional tests are required after reviewing these reports.

items.q: Should I get a second opinion before starting apatinib?
items.a: A second opinion can be helpful before starting apatinib, especially in the third-line setting where treatment goals and trade-offs need careful discussion. Another specialist may confirm eligibility, review alternatives, or suggest suitable clinical trials based on the patient's reports. This does not guarantee a different recommendation but can support informed decisions. Patients should share complete, up-to-date medical records so any reviewing oncology team can give accurate, individualised advice.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients with apatinib (rivoceranib)?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organize medical reports, identify relevant specialists or treatment centers, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, appointments, travel, visa, and follow-up support. It can help patients explore where apatinib or rivoceranib may be available and gather the information needed for review. Treatment decisions are always made by the qualified oncology team after reviewing the patient's diagnosis, stage, biomarkers, previous treatment, and overall health.
